title: The opportunity
intro: Understand what makes everyday business knowledge valuable—and explain it without the hype.
text: THE IDEA IN TWO SENTENCES Established businesses have years of records that show how real work happens. CloudWRX helps explore whether a buyer may license suitable operational records for AI, subject to fit, rights, privacy review, and the owner’s written agreement. Work leaves a trail of know-how. Decisions in context Email threads and team conversations can show how people solve problems, handle exceptions, and make trade-offs. Processes in motion Tickets, project histories, CRM notes, and SOPs can connect a request to the work and outcome that followed. A possible new use A licensing opportunity depends on the records, their permitted use, their quality, and what a buyer needs. Your role is the relationship. You open the door Explain the opportunity in plain language. Ask a few high-level fit questions. Disclose that you are a referral partner. Introduce the owner to the provider team. title: Who to target
intro: Look for digital history, useful operational context, and an owner who can authorize a review.
text: 20+ people working at desks 3+ years accessible business records 5+ tools brochure prospecting guideline US / CA current provider geography The provider currently lists US or Canada, 3+ years, and 20+ desk staff. The brochure also suggests 5+ software systems and English-language records. These are screening guides; the provider decides actual fit. Three questions to start the conversation. “About how many people work at a desk, on shared email and software?” Focus on people whose work creates shared digital records, rather than total field headcount. “What software runs the business, and how long have you used it?” Ask about email, chat, CRM, tickets, project tools, and the history they still retain. “Who would decide on licensing company records?” Bring that person—and relevant IT or legal colleagues—into the discovery conversation. Where to look first Software & IT SaaS, MSPs, development agencies, cybersecurity, analytics, and cloud consultancies. Finance & accounting CPA, bookkeeping, tax advisory, fractional CFO, payroll, valuation, and back-office firms. Legal Business law, estate planning, litigation support, and other practices with separable operational workflows. Operations & logistics Freight, 3PL, distribution, warehousing, procurement, manufacturing support, and field service operations. Energy & industrial Engineering, equipment service, energy logistics, utility support, maintenance, and safety consultancies. Service & back office Consulting, BPOs, staffing, property management, agencies, associations, and administrative operations. Smaller specialist firms The brochure notes possible exceptions for law and accounting firms. Ask the provider about current exceptions; do not present an internal headcount example as approval. Rights and confidentiality review still apply. Reasons to explore Years of cloud-based records. Regular help-desk, CRM, or project activity. Documented decisions, handoffs, and approvals. An authorized decision maker willing to review. An upcoming sale, merger, closure, or system migration. Reasons to pause Little retained digital history. Unclear ownership or permission. Mostly field crews with few shared systems. Privileged, medical, minors’, classified, or export-controlled material. No clear way to separate restricted information. Ask about categories, not contents Examples include email, Slack or Teams, Jira or Zendesk, CRM, SOPs, code history, and consented recordings. Do not request samples yourself. The privacy lesson explains what to exclude.

title: Objection handling
intro: Welcome the question, answer briefly, and bring specific issues to the right person.
text: Find an owner question 16 questions This sounds too good to be true. + That is fair. This is a possible licensing opportunity, not a promised payout. The provider can explain the process and written terms, and you decide whether it fits. What happens to my data? What about privacy? + Ask about exclusions, de-identification, human review, approved recipients, and use and retention limits. Removing identifiers does not make every dataset anonymous or risk-free. Involve your counsel and IT team. Do you need access to our systems? + Not for an introduction. Start with a description of systems and records. Do not send me files or credentials. If you proceed, authorized staff should agree with the provider on any later export or access. Is this legal? + That depends on rights, contracts, privacy obligations, professional rules, and the proposed use. Have your counsel review the scope and agreement. A referral partner cannot determine legal clearance. Am I selling my data or losing ownership? + The opportunity is described as licensing for an agreed use. Review ownership, exclusivity, permitted use, and any sublicensing rights in the actual terms before deciding. Could this help a competitor? + Ask who can receive or use records, whether that use could affect your business, and what exclusions or restrictions can be agreed. Do not assume anonymity eliminates competitive risk. What does it cost? + The playbook describes no upfront owner fee and a success-based model. Ask the provider to identify all fees, deductions, and conditions in writing before proceeding. How much is it worth? + It depends on the records, rights, quality, uniqueness, and buyer demand. A public range or example is not an offer for your company. The provider must review the opportunity. How long does it take to get paid? + The current provider page says usually 90–120 days after signing; the original brochure used about 60 days from introduction. Neither guarantees a date. Confirm the buyer’s process and payment terms. Which AI labs are involved? + I would not name a buyer for your company before a real proposal exists. Ask the provider to identify the proposed buyer and permitted use when you review an offer. Our records are a mess. We are not technical. + Start with a high-level list of tools and approximate years of history. The provider can explain what is useful and what work would be needed. You do not need to prepare files for me. How much work is this for my team? + The first discussion is intended to be short. A transaction can require substantial IT, rights, privacy, and legal review. Ask for a realistic scope and division of responsibilities before committing. Why not go directly to an AI lab? + You can evaluate different routes. A provider may help with preparation and buyer discussions. Compare services, fees, and terms rather than assuming one route guarantees a better result. Can you just send information? + Of course. I can send the overview or my client link. If you would like a follow-up, what time and channel work for you? I need to talk with my partner, CFO, or lawyer. + Absolutely. Invite them to the discussion so everyone hears the same answers. Include the people responsible for the business, records, and obligations. I am not interested. + Understood, and thanks for letting me know. I will close the loop. Leave the door open without pushing, and honor any request to stop contact. No matching questions. Try a broader word or clear the search.

title: Privacy & protection
intro: Know the questions to ask. Keep sensitive information out of a referral conversation.
text: Redaction and transformation do different jobs. REDACTION Remove a detail “Alice emailed Bob about Acme Corp.” [REDACTED] emailed [REDACTED] about [REDACTED]. Useful when the detail should not appear in the shared record. TRANSFORMATION Substitute a detail “Alice emailed Bob about Acme Corp.” Andrea emailed Brian about Company A. Consistent substitutes can preserve relationships and context. A substitute is not a guarantee Both examples are illustrative. Substitution can be pseudonymization rather than anonymization. Context, rare events, linked records, and retained keys may still permit identification. Ask how residual risk is assessed for the specific dataset. The review described in the playbook Automated preparation Identify sensitive fields and apply agreed removal or transformation rules. Ask what the tools can and cannot detect. Human review Review outputs and exceptions. Ask about sampling, acceptance criteria, and how missed information is handled. Controlled handling Confirm recipients, permissions, transfer methods, retention, and deletion in the process and agreement. Keep restricted material out of scope. Passwords, credentials, and API keys. Personal identifiers, account and payment-card details. Privileged legal documents and confidential client material. Medical records, protected health information, minors’ data, and biometric data. Classified or export-controlled information. Third-party material the company has no right to license. Owners and advisors must determine which records can be used. A record’s presence in company systems does not by itself establish a right to license it. Questions for the owner’s review What is included and excluded? Agree on scope and exclusion rules before preparation. Who approves the sample and buyer? Document review checkpoints and who has authority. What use does the license allow? Review training, evaluation, onward transfer, sublicensing, re-identification restrictions, retention, and deletion. What if a problem is found? Clarify how preparation pauses, issues are corrected, and incidents are handled. The partner’s boundary Discuss categories and questions. Let the owner, authorized IT team, legal advisors, and provider handle actual records and contractual decisions. This training does not establish legal compliance.
